cards.title: 6.1.1 Growth and Development in Flowering Plants
body: In plants growing points are found at the tip of stems and roots.
In special circumstances the young (immature) cells of a root, stem or leaf may become active and divide to form a new root or a new shoot.

cards.title: 6.1.2 Seed Dormancy and Germination
body: Dormant seeds are seeds which remain viable (alive) though metabolically inactive and incapable of germination under the conditions normally favourable for the species.
In other words, the seed is “asleep”, waiting for the ideal conditions to awaken.

cards.title: 6.1.3 Plant Growth Hormones
body: Plant hormones are chemical substances that affect a plant’s ability to respond to its environment.
Plant hormones are also known as plant growth regulators because they can stimulate or inhibit plant growth.

cards.title: Plant systems
body: Xylem: water/minerals up. Phloem: sugars both ways. Transpiration pull helps xylem flow.
Photosynthesis in chloroplasts: CO₂+H₂O → glucose+O₂ (light).

cards.title: Tropisms

Geotropism: roots down, shoots up.

cards.title: 6.1 Plant Tissues, Growth, and Hormones
body: 6.1 Plant Tissues, Growth, and Hormones

**Plant Tissues and Developmental Endocrinology** is the scientific study of the specialized cellular layers (meristematic, simple, and complex tissues) that construct the plant body, the physiology of seed dormancy and germination, and the regulatory roles of plant hormones (phytohormones) in governing growth and environmental responses.

Like multicellular animals, flowering plants (angiosperms) exhibit high levels of structural organization. Their bodies are divided into two primary systems: the below-ground root system and the above-ground shoot system. Plant growth originates in localized regions containing young, actively dividing, undifferentiated cells called meristems (or meristematic tissues). Apical meristems located at the tips of roots and shoots drive primary growth (lengthening), while lateral meristems (such as vascular

cards.title: Plant Systems
body: A seed is a protective package containing a dormant plant embryo and a food reserve (stored in cotyledons or endosperm). Seed dormancy is a vital evolutionary adaptation that halts active embryonic growth and metabolic processes, allowing the seed to survive adverse environmental conditions like dry seasons or freezing winter temperatures. Germination is the resumption of embryonic growth after dormancy is broken. This process begins with imbibition—the passive absorption of significant amounts of water through an opening called the micropyle. This water swells the seed, activates metabolic enzymes, and bursts the protective outer coat (testa), allowing the embryonic root (radicle) to emerge.

cards.title: Plant Systems
body:
| Plant Tissue Group | Specific Cell Types | Structural / Physiological Characteristics | Primary Physiological Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Meristematic** | Apical & Lateral meristems | Small, undifferentiated cells with thin primary walls | Active cell division driving primary and secondary growth |
| **Parenchyma** | Chlorenchyma / Storage cells | Thin primary walls, large central vacuoles, living | Photosynthesis, food/water storage, and tissue regeneration |
| **Collenchyma** | Collenchyma cells | Elongated cells with unevenly thickened primary walls | Provides flexible, mechanical support in young stems and leaves |
| **Sclerenchyma** | Fibers & Sclereids | Thick secondary walls containing lignin, dead at maturity | Provides rigid, high-strength structural support to mature organs |
| **Xylem** | Vessels & Tracheids | Thick-walled, hollow, elongated, dead at maturity |

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which of the following plant tissues contains actively dividing undifferentiated cells responsible for primary and secondary growth?

steps.text: Parenchyma, sclerenchyma, and dermal tissues are permanent differentiated tissues.
Meristematic tissue consists of young, actively dividing, undifferentiated cells located at growing points (apical and lateral) that drive plant growth.
Therefore, the correct choice is **Meristematic tissue**.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which plant hormone is responsible for cell elongation, phototrophic bending, and maintaining apical dominance?

steps.text: Gibberellins stimulate stem growth. ABA inhibits growth. Ethylene ripens fruit.
Auxin (primarily Indoleacetic acid, or $$IAA$$) regulates apical dominance, cell elongation, and phototropic curvature.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which leaf mesophyll layer consists of tightly packed, vertically elongated cells optimized for capturing sunlight for photosynthesis?

steps.text: The leaf interior (mesophyll) is divided into palisade and spongy layers.
The palisade mesophyll is located on the upper surface, consisting of tightly packed, columnar cells rich in chloroplasts to maximize solar energy capture.
Therefore, the correct choice is **Palisade mesophyll**.

body: Plant cells are formed at meristems, and then develop into cell types which are grouped into tissues and tissue systems.

Once cells produced by meristems mature, they differentiate into permanent tissues. Simple permanent tissues are composed of a single cell type and include parenchyma, collenchyma, and sclerenchyma. Parenchyma is the most abundant and versatile cell type, possessing thin, flexible primary walls; they function in photosynthesis (when packed with chloroplasts as chlorenchyma), food/water storage, and tissue repair. Collenchyma cells have unevenly thickened primary walls and provide flexible structural support to actively growing shoots and leaves. Sclerenchyma cells have thick, rigid secondary walls impregnated with lignin; they are typically dead at maturity and provide heavy structural support in the form of fibers or sclereids.

cards.title: Plant Systems
body: Plant growth and environmental responses are regulated by five major classes of plant hormones (phytohormones). Auxins (primarily indoleacetic acid, or $$IAA$$) are synthesized in apical meristems and are responsible for cell elongation, apical dominance (suppressing lateral bud growth), and phototropism (growing toward light). Gibberellins promote stem elongation by stimulating both cell division and elongation, break seed dormancy to initiate germination by activating hydrolytic enzymes, and promote fruit development.

cards.title: Plant Systems
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The synthetic auxin **2,4-D** is widely used in agriculture as a selective herbicide. It selectively triggers rapid, uncontrolled, and fatal growth in broad-leaved dicot weeds (such as dandelions) while leaving narrow-leaved monocot crops (such as wheat, corn, and grasses) entirely unharmed.

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily remember the functional differences between the five major plant hormones, use the phrase: **A**uxins **A**rch (bend/elongate), **G**ibberellins **G**row (stem/seed), **C**ytokinins **C**leave (divide cells), **A**bscisic **A**rrest (dormancy/stress), and **E**thylene **E**xits (ripening/shedding).

cards.title: 6.2 Plant Organs and Transport Systems
body: 6.2 Plant Organs and Transport Systems

**Organ Anatomy and Vascular Translocation** is the anatomical study of roots, stems, leaves, and flowers in angiosperms, and the physical mechanisms (transpiration pull, root pressure, and bulk flow) that drive the transport of water, minerals, and manufactured sugars through vascular tissues.

The roots anchor the plant securely in the soil and absorb water and dissolved minerals. Dicotyledonous plants typically possess a taproot system (a single dominant primary root with branching lateral roots), while monocotyledonous plants possess a fibrous root system (dense, equal-sized adventitious roots). A longitudinal section of a growing root tip reveals four distinct regions: the protective root cap, the zone of cell division (apical meristem), the zone of elongation (where cells absorb water and rapidly lengthen), and the zone of maturation

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which simple permanent plant tissue is characterized by living cells with unevenly thickened primary cell walls that provide flexible support?

steps.text: Parenchyma has thin primary walls. Sclerenchyma has thick, rigid lignified secondary walls.
Collenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened primary cell walls that provide structural, flexible support to young, actively growing stems and petioles.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: What is the primary function of Abscisic Acid (ABA) in plants during environmental stress?

steps.text: **Step 1: Define ABA as a stress hormone**
$$ABA$$ is synthesized in plastids and acts as a key stress signaler.
Under drought stress, $$ABA$$ causes potassium ions to exit guard cells, closing stomata to prevent transpiration water loss, and maintains seed dormancy.
Therefore, the correct choice is **To maintain seed dormancy and trigger rapid stomatal closure during water deficit**.

lessons.title: The Root: Primary Structure and Function

cards.title: 6.3.1 Tap and Fibrous Root Systems
body: The two principal functions of roots are the absorption of water and minerals, and anchorage.
When the seed germinates, the radicle is usually the first structure to appear; it becomes the first root and is called the primary root.

cards.title: 6.3.2 Root Growth Regions
body: Root Cap: The root cap is made up of parenchyma cells that form an inverted cup-shape, as a covering for the tip of each root.
The outer part of the root cap is rough and uneven because its cells are constantly being worn away as the root pushes through the soil.

cards.title: 6.3.3 Internal Structure of the Root
body: In cross section, a root has an epidermis, cortex, endodermis and pericycle, and xylem and phloem.
The cortex is the tissue immediately inside the epidermis and functions in storing food.

cards.title: Plant Systems
body: Complex permanent tissues are composed of multiple cell types working together to perform transport functions. The two primary complex tissues are xylem and phloem, which make up the plant's vascular system. Xylem is responsible for transporting water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the shoots. It consists of hollow, dead conducting cells: tracheids (long, tapered cells) and vessels (wider, continuous tubes with open ends). Phloem is responsible for transporting manufactured organic nutrients (sugars) bidirectionally throughout the plant. It consists of living conducting cells: sieve-tube elements (which lack nuclei at maturity) and adjacent companion cells that provide metabolic support.

cards.title: Plant Systems
body: Cytokinins promote cell division (cytokinesis) and delay aging (senescence) in plant organs, often working in a precise ratio with auxins to direct root and shoot development. Abscisic acid ($$ABA$$) acts primarily as a growth inhibitor; it maintains seed dormancy and triggers the rapid closing of stomata to conserve water during drought stress. Ethylene, unique as a gaseous hormone, accelerates fruit ripening and triggers abscission (the shedding of leaves and fruits).

cards.title: Plant Systems
body:
1. Explain the physiological mechanism by which auxin ($$IAA$$) causes a plant stem to bend toward a unilateral light source (phototropism).
   * **Answer**: Unilateral light causes auxin to migrate from the illuminated side to the shaded side of the stem tip. The higher concentration of auxin on the shaded side stimulates active proton pumping into the cell walls, lowering the pH, loosening cellulose microfibrils, and driving rapid cell elongation on the shaded side, causing the stem to bend toward the light.

In cross-section, a mature dicot root has an outer epidermis, a thick storage cortex of parenchyma cells, a single-layered endodermis containing a waterproof Casparian strip that regulates mineral entry, a pericycle (where lateral roots originate), and a central vascular core containing a star-shaped arrangement of xylem with phloem tucked in between. A monocot root has a central core of parenchyma called pith surrounded by vascular bundles. In stems, dicots arrange their vascular bundles in a neat ring surrounding a central pith, whereas monocots have vascular bundles scattered throughout the ground tissue.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: What is the primary physical process that initiates seed germination by causing the dry seed to absorb water passively?

steps.text: Before cellular metabolism can begin, a dry seed must absorb water to activate cellular enzymes.
This passive absorption of water through the micropyle, which swells the cotyledons and bursts the seed coat, is called imbibition.

cards.title: Study Notes worked
cards.problem: Which single layer of cells in the root cross-section contains the waterproof Casparian strip that regulates mineral entry?

steps.text: Water absorbed by roots passes through the epidermis and cortex toward the vascular cylinder.

The endodermis is the innermost cortical layer. Its cell walls contain suberin (the Casparian strip), which blocks apoplastic water flow, forcing water to pass through cell membranes to regulate mineral entry.
